title: The Jackal and the Proud Lion
source_collection: Panchatantra — Ryder Translation
raw_text: In a great forest there lived a lion named Durgama, the Unapproachable, who slew every living creature he chanced to meet. The animals of the forest held a parliament and resolved that each day one of their number should be offered to the lion as his appointed meal, so that the rest might live in peace. Day by day the lion received his portion without labour. When it came the turn of the hare, that small creature walked very slowly toward the lion's den, arriving late. The lion, enraged by the delay, demanded an explanation. The hare replied with all humility: Your Majesty, I was set upon on the road by another lion of enormous size who declared himself the true lord of this forest. He showed me a great stone well near the silk-cotton tree and said his fortress was within it. Only by pleading your mighty name was I able to escape. The lion, inflamed with pride and rage, commanded the hare to lead him to this rival. They came to the deep stone well. The lion gazed in and saw his own reflection snarling back at him. With a mighty roar he leaped into the well to slay his enemy, and there he drowned. The animals rejoiced, and the hare was honoured for his wisdom.

title: The Hare and the Vain Lion
source_collection: Hitopadesha — Sir Edwin Arnold Translation
raw_text: There was once a lion named Pratapasinha, the Valorous Sun, who ruled the great forest near the Godavari river and killed every beast he encountered. The animals gathered together and came before him saying: O King, if you devour us all today, there will be none left to rule tomorrow. Let us instead send you one creature each sunrise as your rightful meal, and your domain will remain ever full of subjects. The lion agreed. When the hare's day arrived, he walked slowly and meditated upon a plan. He came to the lion when the sun was already high. The lion roared in fury. The hare said: Lord of beasts, I was detained by a second lion of fearsome aspect who dwells within the great marble cistern near the banyan grove. He seized me and said he would send you a message: that this forest is his and you are an intruder. I escaped only by swearing I would bring you his challenge. The lion commanded the hare to show him this rival. They came to the stone cistern. The lion peered in and saw a great lion peering back, teeth bared, eyes blazing. He leaped in to destroy his enemy and was swallowed by the deep water. All the forest creatures praised the clever hare.

title: Sihacamma Jataka — The Wise Hare and the Arrogant Lion
source_collection: Jataka Tales — E.B. Cowell Translation, Vol. II
raw_text: At that time the Bodhisatta was born as a hare in a certain woodland near the Himalayan foothills. A lion named Kharadathika, he of the sharp teeth, terrorised every creature in the forest. The animals entered into a compact with the lion, sending him one creature daily so the rest might live. When the day arrived for the hare to present himself, the Bodhisatta set out slowly, thinking of the means of destroying the tyrant. He came before the lion in the late afternoon. The lion bellowed: Miserable creature! You arrive when the sun is already departing! Know that for this crime I shall slay you and then slay every beast besides! The hare replied: Great king, I was sent with four companions, but a second lion, monstrous in size, waylaid us near the deep forest well. He devoured my companions and demanded that you come to do battle with him. The lion snarled: Show me this creature! They went to the well. The lion looked in and saw his own form reflected. He roared. The echo returned his roar from below. Convinced his enemy lay within, the lion dived in and perished. Thus through wisdom and not through force did the Bodhisatta free the forest creatures from their oppressor.

title: The Rabbit Who Slew the Lion King
source_collection: Kathasaritsagara — Tawney Translation
raw_text: In the great Vindhya forest there reigned a lion of ferocious appetite who permitted no beast to live without his permission. The creatures of the wood came to a counsel and determined that each day one amongst them should walk willingly to the lion as his meal. For a long season this arrangement held. When the rabbit's turn came, he appeared before the lion not at midday as custom demanded, but when the shadows had grown long. He explained: O Lion, I was hurrying to you with utmost speed when I was challenged near the ancient stone well by a lion of vast size. He told me he is the true sovereign of these lands. He lives within the well, he said, for it opens into a vast underground kingdom. He threatened to devour me unless I agreed to lure you to him. The lion commanded the rabbit to lead the way. He peered into the dark depths of the well and beheld a terrible lion staring up at him. He hurled himself in to destroy his rival and was seen no more. The rabbit returned to the assembly of forest creatures and was celebrated as their deliverer.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
source_collection: Panchatantra — Ryder Translation
raw_text: On the bank of a great river there grew a rose-apple tree, and in it lived a monkey named Raktamukha, the Red-Face. In the river below dwelt a crocodile named Karalamukha with his wife. Each day the monkey would drop rose-apples into the river for the crocodile, and so a great friendship arose between them. One day the crocodile's wife said: Husband, if this monkey eats such sweet fruit every day, his heart must be sweeter still. Bring me his heart and I shall eat it. The crocodile, although grieved, promised to obey his wife. He went to the monkey and invited him to visit his home across the river, offering to carry him on his back. When they were in the middle of the river the crocodile said: Friend, my wife desires your heart. I am sorry, but I must take your heart to her. The monkey replied without missing a beat: Dear crocodile, if only you had told me! Monkeys do not carry their hearts within them — we leave them hanging in the trees. Take me back to the rose-apple tree and I will fetch my heart down for you. The foolish crocodile turned back. When the monkey reached the bank he leaped into the tree and said from above: Go home, crocodile. A creature who would betray a friend is no friend of mine.

title: Sumsumara Jataka — The Crocodile Who Wanted the Monkey's Heart
source_collection: Jataka Tales — E.B. Cowell Translation, Vol. I
raw_text: When the Bodhisatta had been born as a monkey, he lived in great trees on the bank of the Ganga and ate the sweet fruits thereof. A crocodile and his mate lived below the waterline and the crocodile often received fruits thrown down by the Bodhisatta. The crocodile's wife grew jealous of this friendship and said she wished to eat the monkey's heart, believing it must be sweet from such constant consumption of sweet fruits. The crocodile offered to bring the monkey across the river to meet his family. Midstream he confessed his wife's desire. The Bodhisatta, perfectly composed, replied: Friend, I am distressed that you did not tell me before our departure. My heart is not with me — I left it hanging in my fig tree, as we monkeys are accustomed to do. Row me back and I will retrieve it willingly. The crocodile, not perceiving the deception, turned his course. The moment he touched the bank the Bodhisatta leaped to safety. Looking back, he said: You have acted from treachery, and treachery repays the treacherous. My heart is within me, as it has always been. Thus the Bodhisatta through swift thinking preserved his life.

title: The Ape and the Mugger Crocodile
source_collection: Hitopadesha — Sir Edwin Arnold Translation
raw_text: Upon the wide river Gandaki there stood a tall jambu tree whose berries were sweet as sugarcane. In its branches dwelt an ape who befriended a mugger crocodile living in the depths below. Each morning the ape would toss ripe berries into the water. The crocodile brought some home to his wife. She ate and said: If the berries that nourish this ape are so sweet, how much sweeter must be his liver. Obtain his liver for me and I shall cook it with spices. The crocodile with a heavy heart invited the ape to cross the river on his back. Mid-river he revealed the plot. The ape thought swiftly and said: You should have told me before! Apes keep their livers not within their bodies but wrapped carefully in fig leaves and stored in the fork of their home tree. Return me to my tree and you shall have the liver I set aside there this very morning. The crocodile turned. The moment they touched the bank the ape sprang up. He said from the branches: Betrayal breaks friendship. Never come here again. The crocodile went home empty and ashamed.

title: The Brahmin, the Mongoose, and the Serpent
source_collection: Panchatantra — Ryder Translation
raw_text: A Brahmin named Deva Sarman lived with his wife and a baby son. His wife had reared a young mongoose as a pet, and the mongoose played daily with the infant child. One day the wife went to fetch water and left the Brahmin to watch the baby. The Brahmin was called away to beg alms and left the mongoose to guard the child. While he was gone a great black serpent slithered from the wall and made toward the cradle. The mongoose attacked the serpent, and after a fierce struggle, killed it. He ran to meet his mistress at the doorway, his mouth stained red with blood. The wife screamed: You have killed my child! and struck the mongoose dead with her heavy water-pot. She rushed inside and found her child sleeping peacefully, the dead serpent lying nearby in pieces. She wept for the mongoose all her remaining days. Act not in haste, nor judge by outward signs alone, for haste is the seed of ruin.

title: Nakula Jataka — The Mongoose Who Saved the Child
source_collection: Jataka Tales — E.B. Cowell Translation, Vol. I
raw_text: In former times the Bodhisatta was born as a mongoose in the household of a wealthy family in Baranasi. The household had a newborn son. One day as the mother went to bathe at the well she entrusted the child to the mongoose. A large black snake emerged from a crack in the earthen wall and glided toward the infant's sleeping mat. The mongoose sprang and fought the snake with great ferocity, biting through its neck and killing it. When the mother returned she saw the mongoose at the door with blood on his teeth and paws. Without waiting, without asking, she flung her heavy water jar at the mongoose and killed him. She ran inside, fearing the worst. She found her son asleep and the snake dead beside him. She beat her breast and wept: I have slain my child's defender in my foolishness. Haste in anger destroys what it means to protect.

title: The Jackal and the War Drum
source_collection: Panchatantra — Ryder Translation
raw_text: A hungry jackal wandering in a deserted forest came upon a battlefield that had long been abandoned. He searched for food with no success. Suddenly a tremendous booming sound erupted nearby. Terrified, the jackal froze. He thought: What great beast is this that makes such sound? Shall I flee, or shall I investigate? Mastering his fear he crept toward the sound. He found a great war drum that had been left against the trunk of a fallen tree. Whenever the wind blew the branches of the tree against its skin, the drum boomed and rolled. The jackal laughed at himself for his cowardice. He climbed upon the drum and scratched at its skin. Finding it was made only of leather and bamboo, he gnawed through the skin hoping to find meat and fat inside, since so large a body must contain nourishment. He found nothing but air and empty space. He who lets fear govern reason shall always chase an empty drum.

title: The Frightened Jackal and the Drum of the Forest
source_collection: Hitopadesha — Francis Johnson Translation
raw_text: A certain jackal wandering near an old battlefield heard a tremendous crashing and booming coming from the edge of the forest. He ran in terror, then stopped and reproached himself for cowardice. Summoning courage he crept through the undergrowth toward the sound. He found a great military drum propped against a fallen pipal tree. Each time the wind stirred the branches they struck the drum's taut skin, and it rang out like thunder. The jackal sniffed carefully around the drum, then bit through the skin expectantly. He had supposed that any object making so mighty a sound must contain stores of flesh and marrow. Inside was nothing but wood and hollow air. He sat back on his haunches and reflected: The loudest voice need not indicate the greatest substance. Fear and hunger together had made a thunderous promise that was hollow at its centre.

title: Baital Pachisi — The First Riddle: The Most Devoted Wife
source_collection: Baital Pachisi — Sir Richard Burton Translation
raw_text: King Vikramaditya of Ujjain went at midnight to the burning-ground as a Yogi had instructed him, and took down from the sinsapa tree the corpse in which dwelt the Baital, the Vampire. He set off with it upon his shoulder, and the Baital began to speak. It told him a tale: In the city of Chitrakuta lived a Brahmin named Haridatta who had a beautiful daughter, Madanamanjari. She was sought by three young men of the warrior caste, all equally accomplished, equally devoted. She could not choose. One day she fell ill and died. All three mourned. The first burned his body upon her funeral pyre. The second collected her ashes and set off on pilgrimage. The third made a garland of her ashes and lay down at the shrine of Shiva. Shiva granted his devotion and Madanamanjari was restored to life. Now, said the Baital, which of the three was most truly devoted? Is it the one who died? The one who wandered in grief? Or the one whose prayer brought her back? King Vikramaditya replied without hesitation: The one who lay at the shrine and whose prayer brought her back. The other two grieved as men grieve, but he alone acted on faith. At this answer the Baital flew back to the tree, for the king had been warned: if he spoke, the Baital would escape.

title: Baital Pachisi — The Second Riddle: Three Brothers and the Clay Maiden
source_collection: Baital Pachisi — Sir Richard Burton Translation
raw_text: Again Vikramaditya retrieved the body from the sinsapa tree and again the Baital spoke. In a city there lived a woman who had three sons and died. The eldest fashioned a perfect woman from clay. The second obtained from a sorcerer a book of spells and breathed life into the clay form. The third married her. Now which of the three was the woman's true son, which her husband, and which her creator? Vikramaditya considered: The one who fashioned her from clay did the work of a craftsman but not of a child. The one who breathed life into her acted as a father acts upon a child. The one who married her acted as a husband. Therefore the second is the father, the first is a craftsman with no claim, and the third is the husband. The Baital laughed: You have answered well, O king. But your tongue has moved, and so I return to the tree. Vikramaditya set the body down and went back through the burning-ground for the third time.

title: Simhasana Dvatrimsika — The Throne of Vikramaditya and the Thirty-Two Statuettes
source_collection: Simhasana Dvatrimsika — A.N.D. Haksar Translation
raw_text: King Bhoja of Dhara discovered in a field a great throne with thirty-two statuettes carved into its steps. Whenever he attempted to mount it, one of the statuettes would come to life and tell him a tale of King Vikramaditya's virtue. The first statuette spoke: A hungry traveller once came to Vikramaditya's court and asked for charity. Vikramaditya called his treasurer. The man had nothing to his name. Vikramaditya gave him his own royal turban, set with rubies. The traveller questioned: Why do you give to a stranger what is rightfully your kingdom's treasury? Vikramaditya replied: What is mine is what I can give. What I cannot give is not truly mine. Only if you can equal such generosity may you sit upon this throne, the statuette told Bhoja. Bhoja descended in humility.

title: Birbal's Khichdi — The Warmth of a Distant Flame
source_collection: Birbal Folklore — North India Oral Tradition
raw_text: In the reign of Emperor Akbar, a poor man bet the court that he could stand in the freezing Yamuna river all night without fire. He did so and came to the court shivering but triumphant, saying he had watched a distant lamp burning in a courtier's house across the river. Akbar ruled that since the man had received warmth from the distant lamp, he had not truly stood without fire and had therefore lost his bet. The man went away weeping. Birbal, the emperor's wisest minister, refused to attend court that day. Akbar summoned him. Birbal said he was busy cooking khichdi. Days passed and Birbal did not appear. Finally Akbar went to Birbal's house and found a pot of rice suspended on a tall pole, with a small candle burning on the ground far below it. Has your khichdi cooked yet? Akbar demanded. Birbal replied: Your Majesty, if a man can receive warmth from a lamp burning across a wide river, then surely this rice will cook from this candle far below. Akbar understood his injustice and rewarded the poor man.

title: Birbal Counts the Crows
source_collection: Birbal Folklore — North India Oral Tradition
raw_text: One morning Emperor Akbar was watching the crows in his garden and was seized by curiosity. He commanded his courtiers to tell him exactly how many crows lived in his kingdom. The courtiers were baffled. Birbal stepped forward and said without hesitation: Your Majesty, there are ninety-five thousand, four hundred and sixty-three crows in your kingdom. Akbar asked: How do you know this so exactly? Birbal replied: Your Majesty, please have them counted. If there are more, then some of the crows have brought their relatives from a neighbouring kingdom for a visit. If there are fewer, some of our crows have gone abroad on holiday. Akbar burst into laughter and rewarded Birbal with a diamond. The quality of a wise answer is not always its precision but its unassailability.

title: Birbal and the Line That Must Be Shorter
source_collection: Birbal Folklore — North India Oral Tradition
raw_text: Emperor Akbar drew a long line on the floor of the court and asked his courtiers to make it shorter without touching it or erasing any part of it. All were stumped. Birbal came forward and drew a longer line next to the emperor's line. The emperor's line was now the shorter of the two. Akbar said: You have made my line shorter without touching it. You are truly the jewel of my court. Birbal answered: Your Majesty, the greatest diminishment does not come from erasing a thing but from placing beside it something greater. This principle holds in all matters of governance.

title: Tenali Raman and the Thieves in the Garden
source_collection: Tenali Raman Stories — South India Oral Tradition
raw_text: Tenali Raman, the court jester and poet of King Krishnadevaraya, heard that thieves had been raiding his garden and orchard at night. He could not afford guards. That night he went out at dusk and began dropping large round stones into the dry well at the garden's centre, counting loudly: one, two, three, four... The thieves were hiding in the bushes and heard him. They whispered: He is dropping treasure into the well! When Tenali went inside, the thieves crept out and spent the entire night hauling up stone after stone from the well. In this effort they not only retrieved no treasure but drew up enough water to thoroughly irrigate the garden. In the morning Tenali came out, saw his garden beautifully watered, and thanked the thieves for their service. The story spread and no thief troubled his garden thereafter.

title: Tenali Raman and the Cursed Cat
source_collection: Tenali Raman Stories — South India Oral Tradition
raw_text: The court priests complained to King Krishnadevaraya that Tenali Raman's cat had eaten the sacred milk set out for the temple deity. The priests demanded the cat be punished and an enormous fine be paid. Tenali Raman appeared before the king with the cat. He said: Your Majesty, the priests insist the cat drank a pot of milk. I have trained the cat carefully in spiritual matters. Perhaps your majesty will permit a test. He held up a pot of hot milk. The cat, remembering it had burnt its tongue, backed away and refused to touch it. Tenali said: You see, Your Majesty, the cat is now afraid of milk. How can a creature afraid of milk have drunk the priests' offering? Either the priests kept their milk so cold as to be spiritually suspect, or some other creature drank it. The king laughed and dismissed the case. The priests were confounded.

title: Tenali Raman and the Needy Brahmins
source_collection: Tenali Raman Stories — South India Oral Tradition
raw_text: King Krishnadevaraya announced that he would donate a cow to every Brahmin in the kingdom on the occasion of a festival. The Brahmins were overjoyed. Tenali Raman quietly prepared. When the day of the gift-giving arrived, thousands of Brahmins gathered. Tenali brought out his gift — a very old, thin cow with a broken horn, a lame foot, and barely any milk left. He offered this cow to the foremost priest of the assembly and bowed deeply. The priest was furious: Is this fit to offer to a man of learning? Tenali smiled: Revered sir, the king said donate a cow. He did not specify which kind. A cow is a cow. Is it not all the same if she fulfils the sacred requirement? The king laughed so hard he spilled his wine, and thereafter was careful to specify what he gave.

title: Daddara Jataka — The Hare Who Shook the Earth
source_collection: Jataka Tales — E.B. Cowell Translation, Vol. I
raw_text: When the Bodhisatta was a lion, he dwelt near a great nyagrodha tree. Nearby a hare sat beneath a palmyra tree thinking fearful thoughts: What if the earth were to break apart? What would happen to me? At that moment a large ripe coconut fell to the earth with a tremendous crash. The hare leaped up and ran, crying out: The earth is breaking! Other animals saw him running and joined the stampede. Deer, boar, buffalo, rhinoceros, elephant — all fled in a great thundering mass. The Bodhisatta, the lion, stood in their path atop a hill and roared three times. The animals halted. He asked the hare: What did you hear? What did you see? Together they returned to the palmyra tree and found only the fallen coconut. The lion spoke to all the animals: A sound, a rumour, an unseen fear nearly drove ten thousand beasts over a cliff. Question what you hear. Seek out the source before you act upon terror.

title: The Four Treasure-Seeking Brahmins
source_collection: Panchatantra — Ryder Translation
raw_text: Four Brahmin friends who were great scholars but very poor resolved to travel to a foreign land and seek their fortune. As they journeyed through a forest, they came to a crossroads where they found a thread of magical silk dropped by a Vidyadhara spirit. When each held a piece of the thread it pointed the way to treasure. Three of them followed their threads deep into the mountain and each discovered a mine: one of silver, one of copper, one of gold. Satisfied, they urged the fourth to come away with what they had found. But the fourth's thread continued to lead him onward, and though his friends mocked him, he followed it further still. It led him to a man sitting under a miraculous tree, naked, with a wheel of sharp blades spinning on his head. The fourth Brahmin said: Sir, why do you sit here with that wheel upon your head? Instantly the wheel flew from the man's head to the Brahmin's. The man explained: You have broken the spell. The wheel stays until someone else wanders here asking the same question. Only then does it fly to them. Those who pursue knowledge past all discomfort bear its burdens as well as its gifts.

title: Raja Vikram and the Forest Goddess
source_collection: Simhasana Dvatrimsika — Regional Rajasthani Variant
raw_text: One of the thirty-two statuettes of King Bhoja's throne told this tale: In the deep forest at the edge of the Vindhya range there was a shrine to the Goddess where the trees themselves were said to speak. King Vikramaditya came to this shrine alone at midnight, as a devotee in need of counsel. The goddess appeared and spoke: Ask one boon, O Vikrama. Ask wealth, or victory, or long life, or wisdom. He replied: I ask for nothing for myself, but grant that the people of Ujjain, who suffer from drought, may have rain. The goddess was silent for a long moment. Then she said: You are the first in seven ages to come here asking for another's sake. Your boon is granted, and another besides. Whatever you require for the welfare of your kingdom shall be given to you before you think to ask for it. Thus Vikramaditya became the greatest patron-king of the age. Generosity before need is the mark of a true sovereign.

title: Ganesha and the Moon's Mockery
source_collection: Sacred Books of the East — Brahma Vaivarta Purana
raw_text: It is told that Ganesha once attended the feast of the Moon-god Chandra and ate so much laddu that he could not walk. Riding on his mouse he returned home when the path was lit only by moonlight, and the mouse stumbled over a snake, sending Ganesha rolling on the ground. His enormous belly burst open and the laddus spilled out on the road. Ganesha collected them and stuffed them back inside, tying the snake around his middle to hold it all together. From behind a cloud Chandra the Moon watched this spectacle and laughed until he shook. Ganesha was furious. He cursed the Moon: You who laughed at Ganesha shall be invisible on all nights, and on Ganesh Chaturthi anyone who looks upon your face shall suffer false accusations. Chandra begged for forgiveness. Ganesha softened the curse: I cannot undo what I spoke, but I grant that you shall wax again and become full each month. Yet on Chaturthi your light shall bring trouble to those who see it. Thus arose the custom of not looking at the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi.

title: Krishna and the Serpent Kaliya of the Yamuna
source_collection: Sacred Books of the East — Bhagavata Purana Book X
raw_text: In the deep pool of the Yamuna river, the many-headed serpent Kaliya made his abode. His venom was so fierce that birds passing over the pool fell dead from the fumes, and the river's waters bubbled and smoked. Krishna, as a young cowherd boy, climbed a great kadamba tree on the bank and plunged into the poisoned waters. Kaliya rose up with all his hoods spread wide, crushing Krishna in his coils. The gopas on the bank wept and prepared to enter the water. But Krishna, laughing, began to grow in size until Kaliya could not hold him. He climbed upon Kaliya's central hood, the largest and most sacred, and danced. As he danced the hood bowed lower and lower until it touched the water. Kaliya's wives came forward and begged for their husband's life. Krishna relented and said: Leave this pool. Go to the sea, where the eagle Garuda fears to come because of the boon I granted. Kaliya bowed his hoods in submission and departed with his family for the ocean. The Yamuna was clean again.

title: Kattahara Jataka — The Clever Parrot and the Greedy Merchant
source_collection: Jataka Tales — E.B. Cowell Translation, Vol. III
raw_text: The Bodhisatta was born as a parrot who lived in the fig tree of a merchant named Suddha. The parrot could speak and was greatly valued. When Suddha died his sons quarrelled over the inheritance and neglected to feed the parrot. The parrot flew to the court of King Brahmadatta and perched on the royal throne. The king asked: From where have you come, wise bird? The parrot told the tale of his master's death and the sons' quarrel. The king summoned the sons. But before they could reply, the parrot spoke: Your Majesty, the question before this court is not who owns the parrot but who shall govern the estate without squandering what their father built. If the law is followed, the eldest takes all. If justice is followed, the estate is held in common until the quarrel is resolved. The king ruled that the estate be held in trust and the brothers first resolve to speak to each other. Wisdom settles what law alone cannot.
